name: VCD (Video CD)
blurb: The cheap disc format that put movies and karaoke in Chinese living rooms in the 1990s
title: What Is a VCD? The Video CD Format That Took Over 1990s China
description: VCD (Video CD) was a 1993 format that stored about 74 minutes of video on an ordinary CD. It was huge in 1990s China and Asia before DVD replaced it.
answer: A VCD, or Video CD, is a disc format created in 1993 by Sony, Philips, Matsushita (Panasonic) and JVC that stores about 74 minutes of MPEG-1 video on an ordinary CD, at roughly VHS quality. It barely registered in the West but took over China and much of Asia: about 8 million VCD players were sold in China in 1997 alone. DVD and then online video replaced it in the 2000s, and disc production in Greater China wound down by the mid-2010s.

sections.h: What it looked like and how it worked
body: A VCD looks exactly like a music CD: 12 cm across, silver on one side. Because one disc holds only 74 to 80 minutes, a feature film usually came on two or sometimes three discs, and you got up halfway through to swap them.

The picture was 352×288 pixels on PAL sets (352×240 on NTSC), about a quarter of standard-definition TV. On the boxy CRT televisions of the time it looked acceptable; up close it broke into blocks. Version 2.0 (1995) added on-screen menus, which made karaoke discs easy to use, and in China a VCD player hooked up to an amplifier and microphones was a fixture of family gatherings.

sections.h: Why it was so big in China
body: Most of Asia went from videotape straight to VCD because CD factories already existed and discs were cheap to press. In China the first domestic VCD player came from Wanyan (万燕), a company in Hefei, which completed it in September 1993; the first 1,000 units sold for 4,000 to 5,000 yuan each, mostly to other electronics makers who took them apart as samples. Wanyan never patented the design, and competitors flooded in.

body: Western sources have also pointed to unlicensed copies as a big reason people bought VCD players, since CD-based discs were easy to duplicate.

DVD did everything VCD did, fitted a whole film on one disc and looked much sharper, and most DVD players could still read VCDs, so switching cost almost nothing. Streaming later replaced DVD in turn.

New VCD players and discs are essentially no longer made. Old discs still play on most DVD players and on computers with a disc drive, though most Blu-ray players dropped VCD support. Players and discs now circulate mainly second-hand and among collectors.

faq.q: What is the difference between VCD and DVD?
faq.a: VCD uses a standard CD and MPEG-1 video at about VHS quality, around 74 minutes per disc. DVD holds far more and looks much sharper, so a full film fits on one disc.

faq.q: Can a DVD player play VCDs?
faq.a: Most DVD players can. Most Blu-ray players cannot, so a DVD player or a computer with a disc drive is the usual way to watch old VCDs.
The format was defined in 1993 by Sony, Philips, Matsushita and JVC. In China, Wanyan in Hefei is credited with the first domestic VCD player the same year.
